questions.q: Why is hardcoding a secret into a .tf file dangerous even in a private repository?
options: It will cause terraform plan to fail immediately
The secret lives forever in Git history and is also written in plain text into the state file
Private repositories automatically encrypt all file contents
Terraform refuses to apply files containing secrets
questions.explain: A hardcoded secret remains in Git history even after rotation, and also gets written into Terraform's state file as part of a resource's attributes, creating a second exposure.

questions.q: How does the lesson recommend supplying a database password to a resource instead of hardcoding it?
options: Typing it directly into a .tfvars file
Reading it at apply time via a data source from Azure Key Vault or AWS Secrets Manager
Emailing it to the team and pasting it in manually each time
Storing it in a comment inside the .tf file
questions.explain: A data source like azurerm_key_vault_secret or aws_secretsmanager_secret_version reads the real secret value live at apply time, so it's never written into any committed file.

questions.q: Where should provider authentication credentials like ARM_CLIENT_SECRET come from?
options: Hardcoded directly inside the provider block
Environment variables, never written into a committed file
The Terraform Registry
A comment at the top of the main.tf file
questions.explain: Provider credentials should be supplied via environment variables rather than hardcoded in a provider block, keeping them out of version control.

questions.q: Which of these should be listed in a Terraform project's .gitignore file?
options: main.tf and variables.tf
*.tfvars, *.tfstate*, and .terraform/
The README.md file
The Terraform Registry source URL
questions.explain: .tfvars files can hold sensitive per-environment values and .tfstate files can contain secrets in plain text as resource attributes, so both — along with the .terraform/ working directory — are excluded from version control.

questions.q: What does a pull request reviewer see when a secret is read via a Key Vault data source, instead of hardcoded?
options: The actual plaintext secret value
A reference to where the secret is stored, not the secret's actual value
Nothing at all — the resource block disappears from the diff
An error message
questions.explain: Because the data source only references the secret's location (vault name and secret name), the actual value never appears in the configuration a reviewer sees.
